How Syria's skies are becoming a new Israel-Turkey battleground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

Breadcrumb
How Syria's skies are becoming a new Israel-Turkey battleground
On 18 August, Israeli fighter jets struck a northwestern Syrian airfield eight times, with Tel Aviv claiming it had pre-empted a Turkish military deployment there.
While the raid did not result in a clash between the two powerful militaries, it nevertheless demonstrated once again how Syria essentially has no control over its airspace.
The airstrikes hit Syria’s Abu al-Duhur Air Base, causing damage but no casualties. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Al-Shaibani said that Turkish military officers visited the site days before the strike. Turkey denied that any delegation was at the base before or during the attack.
Israel claimed Turkey was “on the verge of breaching” the “status quo in security matters” by deploying troops, with Ankara, in turn, describing Israel’s actions as an “unacceptable” and “reckless” threat to regional peace and stability.
Israel previously bombed three airbases in central Syria in April 2025 shortly after Turkey scoped them for potentially deploying forces.
All of these incidents highlight how Syria’s airspace, far from being under its sovereign control, is being contested by its two powerful neighbours who both have large American-equipped air forces.
While Israel appears predominant for now, Turkey may seek to incrementally put constraints on its rival’s aerial supremacy over its southern neighbour.
The battle over Syria's airspace
“The pressure on Israel’s freedom of action in Syria appears to be increasing, even if it has not yet produced a decisive constraint,” Muaz Al Abdullah, Middle East Research Manager at the non-profit Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, told The New Arab.
He noted that the Trump administration has signalled an effort to broaden the Abraham Accords to include Syria “while reducing the scope of conflicts” involving Israel, and the US by extension, in the Middle East. “That diplomatic backdrop coincides with a visible change on the ground,” Abdullah said.
ACLED data shows a notable decline in Israeli airstrikes in Syria since August 2025. Abdullah assesses that this might mean the “operational window” Israel enjoyed since the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad collapsed in December 2024 is beginning to narrow.
“The broader picture, however, is more mixed: Israeli incursions and violence against civilians have continued in uneven but persistent patterns,” Abdullah told The New Arab.
“The shift suggests that Israel may be relying more heavily on ground incursions and other forms of pressure to meet its immediate security objectives,” he added.
“Airstrikes, by contrast, appear to be reserved for moments when those measures are deemed insufficient, as reflected in strikes against Abu al-Duhur, T4, Tadmor, and Hama airbases.”
Replacing Russia's role?
Before the dramatic, free-fall collapse of the brutal Assad regime, Russia officially controlled much of Syria’s airspace around regime-controlled areas and bombed opposition-held regions like Idlib.
Shortly after Russia intervened in Syria’s civil war in September 2015, it established a deconfliction mechanism with Israel, allowing the Israeli Air Force to continue striking suspected Iranian assets in the war-torn country.
US Special Envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said after Israel’s latest strike that the US is working on a similar mechanism between Israel, Turkey, and Syria to reduce the risk of clashes.
Suleyman Ozeren, a lecturer at the American University and senior fellow at the Orion Policy Institute, doesn’t believe this necessarily indicates that Turkey is replacing Russia’s pre-2024 role in Syria or will ever replace it.
“Unlike Russia, Turkey, at least for now, does not appear capable of deterring Israel from carrying out military incursions and strikes inside Syria,” Ozeren told The New Arab.
“Israel’s decision to bomb Abu al-Duhur Air Base, located relatively close to the Turkish-Syrian border, sends a clear message to both the (Syrian President Ahmed) al-Sharaa government and Ankara,” he added.
“Although Turkey responded to the incident with a relatively restrained protest, the strike itself is a troubling indication of how quickly tensions between Israel and Turkey could escalate.”
Deconfliction and de-escalation
Kristin Ronzi, a Middle East and North Africa analyst at the risk intelligence company RANE, says the Turkish-Israeli deconfliction mechanism has already helped de-escalate tensions between the two countries in Syria and “mitigate the risk” of miscalculation.
“As such, Turkey has maintained significant influence over Syrian airspace in the north, while Israel has influence in the south,” Ronzi told The New Arab.
“Even so, the early 18 August Israeli airstrikes against Abu al-Duhur military base in northwestern Syria indicate that Israel is able to extend its operations further into Syria.”
She noted that Barrack’s description of the Israeli strikes as “unnecessary escalation” indicates a limited US tolerance for Israeli airstrikes in Syria in light of warming US-Syria ties and concerns over “Turkish-Israeli frictions”.
“The Trump administration will likely tolerate Israel’s military presence in southern Syria and sporadic ground incursions,” Ronzi said. “But the United States will likely pressure Israel to restrict airstrikes, especially against targets that do not pose a national security threat and risk elevating Syrian-Israeli tensions,” the analyst added.
“Syria will rhetorically reject Israeli violations of its airspace; Syria will be unwilling and unable to effectively control its airspace.”
ACLED’s Abdullah expects that the present status quo of Israel dominating Syria’s southern and central airspace without “direct contestation” with Turkey in central Syria, where there are overlapping areas of influence, will hold.
He recalled Israel’s airstrikes against central Syrian airbases in April 2025 to deter Turkey from establishing any presence.
“The recent strike on Abu al-Duhur does not necessarily represent a contest for dominance between Israel and Turkey in northern Syria,” he said. “It is better understood as a matter of undeclared areas of influence between the two sides, alongside Israeli political objectives tied to the domestic situation inside Israel,” Abdullah added.
“At the same time, where Turkish and Israeli influence in Syria begins and ends is a separate question from Israel’s deterrence strategy of preventing Syria from acquiring an effective, modern air force. That strategy is also one of the reasons behind the Abu al-Duhur strike.”
Ronzi believes Israel will likely reject any Turkish efforts to expand its military influence any further in central Syria.
“Efforts to enhance Syria’s air defence systems would likely be a red line for Israel and Israel would likely obstruct any such efforts, including potentially through pre-emptive airstrikes as Israel has previously done,” she said.
Dreams of a new Syrian air force
Israel’s post-Assad airstrikes destroyed much of what was left of the old regime’s Russian-built air defences and antiquated air force, including its most advanced fighter jets, the Soviet-era MiG-29.
Syria still has some less advanced flyable jets, including Czech-built L-39 light attack aircraft, two of which performed a flyby in a July graduation ceremony for air force cadets, and vintage Soviet-era Su-22s, two of which were spotted over Idlib this August. Israel opposes Syria reconstituting its air force and air defence.
Israel was even concerned that the installation of an HTRS-100 Air Traffic Control Radar System built by Turkey’s Aselsan at Damascus International Airport in January could challenge its air supremacy over Syria.
Ronzi noted that while the HTRS-100 has “commercial and civilian benefits,” it nonetheless “raised Israeli concerns” that it could constrain its military operations.
While Turkey might be able to support “limited Syrian air defence infrastructure,” Abdullah predicts that Israel is likely to “draw a clear line” around any capability that could give Damascus any “meaningful independent control” over its skies.
“Israel’s defence doctrine has increasingly rested on keeping neighbouring states unable to threaten it militarily,” he said.
“In that context, Israel may tolerate Turkey’s deployment of the HTRS-100 radar system at Damascus International Airport, but it is expected to resist any further steps that would allow Syrian forces to own or operate effective air capabilities.”
Ozeren noted that maintaining control over Syrian airspace remains a “key security objective” for Israel that increasingly conflicts with Turkey’s ambitions to expand its influence and presence on the ground in that country.
“Syrian airspace, therefore, is likely to become a major arena in which the competing objectives of Israel and Turkey are tested,” he said. “Without meaningful US intervention, tensions between Israel and Turkey could escalate further.”
“If this competition becomes prolonged, Damascus may eventually seek a more formidable external partner capable of balancing these pressures,” he added. “In that context, a renewed reliance on Russia, though seemingly implausible today, could become a more viable option in the near future.”
ACLED’s Abdullah anticipates that Damascus is likely to turn to Ankara for help in any attempt to rebuild the country’s air force. The expanding partnership between the two makes such cooperation plausible. Turkey could provide pilot training, aircraft, and technical support.
“Recent developments suggest that Syria is already preparing for that possibility,” he said. “The graduation of more than 1,000 non-commissioned officers from the Syrian Air Force Academy points to a broader effort to restore the country’s air arm.”
However, what type of aircraft Syria might seek from Turkey remains uncertain. Furthermore, any procurement decision Damascus ultimately makes will likely be shaped by financial constraints and red lines imposed by Israel.
“Syria may also choose to invest more heavily in unmanned systems rather than trying to rebuild a conventional fighter fleet from the ground up,” Abdullah told The New Arab. “Turkey has a clear advantage in drones, and Syrian forces already have experience that Ankara could help develop,” he added.
“Such a strategy would allow Damascus to challenge Israeli dominance indirectly, without attempting to match Israel in the manned-fighter arena.”
RANE’s Ronzi recalled that Israel’s ferocious attacks on weapons caches and the remnants of Assad’s military following the regime collapse significantly degraded any new military threat his successor can pose to Israel.
“Rebuilding the Syrian Air Force is not likely to be a near-term priority for the interim Syrian government as it faces numerous domestic threats, including the Islamic State, as well as the task of developing new state institutions, over time,” Ronzi said.
Syria will probably attempt to buy new aircraft to improve its military capabilities, most likely from Turkey.
“Even though Israel would maintain a qualitative military edge over any Syrian air force, Israel will be wary of any Syrian effort to rebuild its air force and concerned about the potential that it could eventually be used against Israel,” Ronzi added.
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in the Middle East who writes extensively about the region's affairs, conflicts, and politics

IDF helps Colombians find sufficiently safe homes, delegation deputy head tells 'Post' - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:48 UTC
01:44:48 KST

The IDF has assisted many thousands of Colombians to return to hospitals, schools, and hundreds of other structures partially damaged by the August 10 earthquake that Israeli experts have judged as sufficiently safe, Colombian delegation deputy chief IDF Col. Ehud Moyal told The Jerusalem Post in an exclusive interview on Sunday.
Many thousands of Colombians resided in some hundreds of buildings which initial evaluations by the combined Israeli-Colombian engineering teams have already established are stable, out of a much larger number of structures whose stability still needs to be reviewed, Moyal explained to the Post.
Moyal said that the Israeli delegation would return home in the coming days.
Speaking to the Post from Colombia, Moyal noted that the IDF has already handed over its artificial intelligence and other hi-tech systems to Colombia in recent days regarding the high volume of additional structures still needing to be checked.
The systems the IDF has provided will facilitate mapping out those structures which might be usable, as well as those that need to be demolished – along with how best to carry out demolition processes – and estimates on how long it could take for replacement structures to be built.
Many aspects of the systems are similar to the work carried out by the IDF in Venezuela in July, Moyal said.
The difference is that the Venezuela team consisted of some 35 staffers and engineers, whereas the Colombia team was larger, including over 80 staffers and engineers, with nearly half the team being dedicated to physical rescue attempts.
Venezuela did not request assistance despite larger disaster than Colombia
While the disaster in Venezuela was even larger than the one in Colombia, the government in Caracas did not request a rescue team from Israel, though Colombia did.
According to the IDF Colombia delegation deputy chief, part of the system Israel has provided to Colombia categorizes the structures and then defines them to be treated on different tracks based on the severity of the damage they have suffered.
IDF officials explained to the Post that the disaster management and evaluation systems are designed for intake, tracking, and analysis of harmed structures, especially in Cali, a city of over 2.3 million people.
Most IDF efforts were focused in Cali for over 10 days since shortly after August 13, when the Israeli and Colombian governments authorized deploying the Israeli disaster assistance team, Moyal noted.
In the initial stage, he said, the rescue teams went into action to try to extract any living or deceased persons from disaster areas where the Colombians told them that they had heard voices, breathing, or other sounds indicating possible survivors.
At the second stage, Israeli engineers were deployed to evaluate the sturdiness and stability of the damaged buildings, he stated.
At the third stage, Moyal explained, Israeli engineers carried out a more systematic and technology-guided search for remaining missing persons, including the unrecovered remains of deceased persons.
At certain points, the Israeli team also strategically used drones to aid in their mission.
Moyal said that the decision that the delegation could soon leave came after Israel helped Colombia locate the last remaining missing person. This entailed Israel’s delegation staying on longer than most other delegations.
The IDF deputy chief said that he had met with and received high compliments from Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder and that IDF delegation chief Brig.-Gen. (res.) Yossi Pinto had met with top Colombian national defense officials.
Moyal noted that “Israeli engineers went into a damaged hospital; it was empty because the staff were afraid to go in. They had been told previously that the ceilings and walls were dangerous. They looked at us like we were crazy to go in.”
“But we have the best people, and after 90 minutes, we knew the hospital was fine, with some small reinforcement measures to a pillar here or there. Our engineers provided a great service,” he said.
Further, he recalled, after he told the hospital chief that it could reopen for business, she tracked him down in his car before he pulled away and asked him to come back to speak to her staff.
The entire hospital staff of 60 to 70 employees were standing, waiting to hear from him, and until he explained to them directly why the building was technically safe, they were not ready to return.
Moyal: I received 'many hugs,' attended 'very emotional ceremony'
After his explanation, he “received many hugs and there was an emotional outpouring of gratitude,” he said.
Moyal also noted that he and other IDF team members visited a Cali Jewish synagogue last week where hundreds of families attended “a very emotional ceremony.”
He said that there were “many tears as they sang the prayer for the welfare of IDF soldiers and the Hatikvah national anthem.”
Moreover, he complimented the Foreign Ministry, the Defense Ministry, and others on their intensive cooperation with the IDF rescue and home front teams.

The geopolitical importance of Taiwan and the South China Sea 台灣與南海的地緣政治重要性
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:35 UTC
01:44:35 KST

Taiwan and the South China Sea have long been major issues in US foreign policy, and tensions involving China have kept both in the news in recent months. Beijing claims Taiwan as its own territory and asserts sovereignty over virtually the entire South China Sea, bringing it into confrontation with US allies and partners in the region.
What happens in Taiwan and the South China Sea could have an impact not only on the region but around the world, given their importance to global trade.
The South China Sea, a large body of water bordered by several nations, including China, the Philippines and Vietnam, is one of the world’s key maritime trade routes. Taiwan produces the majority of the world’s advanced semiconductors.
Photo: Google Map 照片：谷歌地圖
“The two are very much connected,” said Hunter S. Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at the Lowy Institute in Australia. “If China were to blockade or seek to forcibly retake Taiwan..., the South China Sea could quickly see spillover effects.”
TAIWAN, A KEY ISSUE IN US-CHINA RELATIONS
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that China claims as its own territory, and Beijing has not renounced the use of force to bring it under its control.
Photo: Reuters 照片：路透
China sends military aircraft, coast guard ships and other vessels around Taiwan on a near-daily basis and periodically conducts large-scale military exercises. Taiwan also regularly holds military drills, including its annual Han Kuang exercises.
The US does not have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan, but maintains extensive unofficial relations and is required under US law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
Under that framework, the US has long been Taiwan’s main informal backer and arms supplier, a relationship that has been a persistent source of tensions with Beijing.
TENSIONS PERSIST IN THE SOUTH CHINA SEA
But China asserts sovereignty over much of the South China Sea, despite a 2016 international arbitration ruling that invalidated Beijing’s expansive maritime claims.
In July, on the 10th anniversary of the ruling, the US, the UK and 12 other countries reiterated that China’s expansive claims have no legal basis. Beijing responded by insisting it would neither accept nor recognize the arbitration decision.
Confrontations in the disputed waters have become more frequent in recent years, particularly involving Chinese, Philippine and Vietnamese forces and fishing fleets.
Chinese coast guard ships and other vessels have used powerful water cannons, military-grade lasers and dangerous blocking maneuvers against Philippine forces and fishermen from other claimant countries. Such confrontations have led to collisions at sea and high-risk encounters in the air.
China has also carried out military drills this month near Scarborough Shoal, a disputed area claimed by both China and the Philippines.
In April, the US and the Philippines kicked off the annual Balikatan military exercises. The drills included mock battle scenarios and live-fire exercises in Philippine provinces facing the disputed South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has said that because the South China Sea is one of the world’s most important maritime commercial corridors, “a conflict could cause major disruptions to the flow of trade.” The sea is connected to surrounding waters through several strategic chokepoints, including the Malacca Strait, which links it to the Indian Ocean and the Taiwan Strait, which connects it to the East China Sea.
What would be the main US interests in the region? For Marston, “the primary objective is preventing China from gaining regional hegemony and dominating the Pacific.”
“The security of Taiwan and its allies such as the Philippines, as well as defense of the first island chain, are integral to this overarching goal,” he said.

台灣與南海長久以來都是美國外交政策中的重大議題，近數個月來，美中之間的緊張局勢更讓台灣與南海不斷成為新聞焦點。北京宣稱台灣是中國領土的一部分，並對幾乎整個南海主張擁有主權，因而與美國在該區的盟友及夥伴陷入對立。
由於台灣與南海對全球貿易的重要性，此處發生的任何事，不僅可能影響區域局勢，也可能會對全世界造成衝擊。
南海是一片由中國、菲律賓、越南等多國環繞的大型海域，也是全球重要的海上貿易航線之一。台灣則生產全球多數的先進半導體。

台灣：美中關係的關鍵議題
台灣是一個自治的民主政體，中國宣稱台灣是其領土的一部分，而北京從未放棄武力犯台的可能性。
中國幾乎每天都派軍機、海警船及其他船隻在台灣周邊活動，並不時舉行大規模軍事演習。台灣也定期舉行軍事演訓，包括每年的漢光演習。
美國與台灣並無正式外交關係，但維持廣泛的非官方關係，而且根據美國法律，美國必須提供台灣自我防衛所需的設備。
在此架構下，美國長期以來一直是台灣主要的非官方支持者與武器供應國，而這樣的關係也一直是美中緊張局勢的緣由之一。
南海緊張局勢持續
另一方面，中國主張對南海大部分海域擁有主權，儘管2016年的國際仲裁案已否定北京對南海範圍廣闊的聲索。
今年7月，在南海仲裁案10週年之際，美國、英國及其他12個國家再次重申，中國對南海廣大範圍的主權主張沒有法律依據。北京則回應稱，既不接受也不承認此仲裁案的裁決。
近年來，南海爭議海域的對峙日益頻繁，尤其是中國、菲律賓與越南的軍警部隊及漁船。
中國海警船及其他船隻曾使用強力水砲、軍用級雷射，以及危險的阻擋與逼近動作，對付菲律賓部隊及其他主權聲索國的漁民。這類對峙已導致海上碰撞，以及空中的高風險接觸。
本月，中國也在黃岩島附近舉行軍事演習。黃岩島是中國與菲律賓均聲稱擁有主權的爭議地區。
今年4月，美國與菲律賓啟動年度「肩並肩」（Balikatan）聯合軍事演習。演習內容包括模擬戰鬥情境及實彈演習，地點位於面向南海爭議海域與台灣海峽的菲律賓省分。

New China rules put Taiwanese at risk: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:35 UTC
01:44:35 KST

Taiwanese visiting China could be detained for being involved in sensitive technology or working for a “hostile company” under Beijing’s new border controls, a national security source said yesterday.
China is on Sept. 15 to implement revised entry and exit regulations that, together with the Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law and proposed revisions to the Administrative Measures for Internet Information Services, would give Chinese authorities broad discretionary powers, the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
People could potentially be detained for being involved in sensitive technology or working for a company deemed “hostile,” reflecting Beijing’s increasingly restrictive security posture amid mounting pressure to maintain domestic stability, they said.
Photo: Bloomberg
China’s State Council issued regulations stipulating that Chinese citizens — which include Taiwanese under Beijing’s China nationality law — who engage in illegal or criminal activities overseas that endanger national security or national interests could be prohibited from leaving China for six months to three years after entering the country.
The rules also stipulate that Chinese citizens who contravene import-export regulations in a way that could endanger national industrial or technological security could be barred from leaving the country.
The national security source said that just as Beijing is using the ethnic unity law to place people it considers “detrimental” to its interests on a list of targets for transnational repression, the new entry and exit rules are similarly open to arbitrary interpretation.
If Chinese authorities determine that a Taiwanese in China is involved in or directly stealing technology, industrial, scientific or military information, or works for a company deemed “hostile,” the person could be unable to return home, or, if they are abroad, their family members in China could be detained to induce them to travel to China, the source said.
Even local governments in border areas are authorized to independently impose exit restrictions, substantially increasing personal safety risks, they added.
The new rules create potential risks to the technology supply chain, as engineers from semiconductor suppliers or IC design companies who travel to China on business could be subjected to movement restrictions or compulsory inspections if their devices contain information about new manufacturing processes or technology development, the source said.
Many multinational companies have already issued internal security guidelines requiring employees traveling to China to carry dedicated “clean” phones and laptops, while prohibiting them from taking routine work or personal devices, they said.
Some foreign businesspeople have stopped using phones installed with WeChat or Sina Weibo immediately after returning to Europe or North America, to guard against the cybersecurity and personal-safety risks posed by Chinese authorities arbitrarily inspecting devices or forcing them to log into social media accounts, the source said.
Beijing is also revising the Administrative Measures for Internet Information Services to regulate online speech and behavior, they said.
That represents not only pressure on Taiwan and other democratic systems, but also a form of “involution” in the rule of law, exposing the enormous pressure Beijing faces to maintain internal stability, they said.
Taiwanese security authorities are working with the Mainland Affairs Council and the Straits Exchange Foundation to develop more detailed safety guidelines for Taiwanese traveling to China, the source said.

‘More power’ says trade group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:34 UTC
01:44:34 KST

Taiwan’s top industrial trade group, the Chinese National Federation of Industries (CNFI, 全國工業總會), urged the government yesterday to diversify the nation’s energy mix, step up support for traditional industries and ease restrictions on migrant workers, as a widening labor shortage threatens to hinder growth beyond the technology sector.
The calls came as Taipei-based CNFI released its annual position paper, pointing to growing strains beneath Taiwan’s booming economy.
While demand for artificial intelligence (AI) products has propelled growth to its fastest pace in decades, traditional industries continue to grapple with labor shortages, rising costs and structural challenges, the group said.
Photo: CNA
“Taiwan cannot rely solely on AI,” CNFI chairman Pan Chun-jung (潘俊榮) said. “Although the technology is playing a key role in boosting Taiwan’s economic growth, the government must also help traditional industries turn around for the health of society as a whole.”
The government expects the economy to expand 11.05 percent this year, driven by exports and investment linked to the global AI boom.
The CNFI backed the government’s plan to encourage heavy electricity users to build their own power-generation facilities or invest in renewable energy, saying the approach was practical and could help ease pressure on the grid.
Photo: Reuters
Stable power supplies have become increasingly critical as AI-related investment drives electricity demand, particularly among semiconductor and other technology companies.
“Industries aren’t afraid of challenges, but they cannot operate in the absence of a stable power supply,” Pan said.
The CNFI said it has long advocated keeping nuclear power as an option as a transitional source of baseload electricity alongside renewable energy, as Taiwan needs a reliable and diversified power supply while reducing carbon emissions.
Pan backed wage increases, saying that profitable companies should not hesitate to share the benefits of economic growth with their workers.
“Workers should take part in corporate gains,” he said.
Taiwan’s minimum monthly wage is expected to surpass NT$30,000 next year, with the government’s wage-review committee scheduled to discuss the issue next month.
Labor shortages ranked as the top concern in the CNFI’s survey, cited by 76.6 percent of respondents, followed by industrial transformation at 75.7 percent and energy policy at 63.1 percent.
Labor shortages have topped the list for three consecutive years.
The CNFI said the widening labor gap has evolved into a systemic crisis that could undermine the foundations of the economy, urging the government to coordinate policies across ministries, identify workforce needs more precisely and implement practical measures.
It pressed for a shift away from the quota-based system for hiring migrant workers toward a more flexible framework that would allow industries facing acute labor shortages to recruit workers based on their actual needs.
The government should double the quota for migrant workers in the general construction sector to 30,000, it said.

Tehran dismisses US economic threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:30 UTC
01:44:30 KST

Iran yesterday dismissed Washington’s declaration of a massive economic pressure campaign, saying it disproved US claims to have dismantled Tehran’s military and nuclear capabilities.
“Your narrative doesn’t add up: you say that Iran’s military power has been ‘dismantled,’ 100% of its military factories ‘destroyed’ and its nuclear program ‘buried,’” Iranian Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi said in a post on X.
Yet, “there is a need for ‘the largest financial invasion in history’ and the mobilization of ‘all institutions and powers’ of the United States! Is this a victory or an admission of America’s defeat?” he added.
Photo: AFP
Earlier, US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent wrote in the Financial Times that Washington was launching the “single greatest financial offensive marshalled against an adversary”— calling it an “economic D-Day.”
Bessent posted on X that the measure came after the US “dismantled Iran’s military capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program.”
He was scheduled to explain the new US sanctions on Iran yesterday.
Meanwhile, the Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs warned countries against joining the US economic campaign, with ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei saying taking part would “definitely have its own consequences.”
The US and Israel triggered the Middle East war with a massive wave of strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, triggering Iranian retaliation across the region. An April 8 ceasefire ended nearly 40 days of intense bombardment, but control over the Strait of Hormuz soon emerged as a key flashpoint in the conflict. Iran has controlled the vital energy conduit since the war began.
Reopening the strait, vital for global oil and gas supplies, has become a US priority, but Tehran insists the waterway will remain closed until Washington lifts its naval blockade on Iranian ports, removes oil sanctions and unfreezes Iranian assets abroad.
Last week, US President Donald Trump announced that Washington would ramp up economic pressure on Iran “on an unprecedented scale.” Washington has urged other governments, including Beijing, to join efforts to further isolate Iran’s economy.
In an article published yesterday in Iran’s Ettela’at newspaper, Iranian Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araghchi said relations with China “have taken on deeper, more structural, and more comprehensive dimensions.”
Iran has faced US and international sanctions since the 1979 Islamic revolution. Trump has repeatedly pursued a “maximum pressure” policy of economic sanctions against Iran, reinstating the approach after returning to office in January last year following a similar campaign during his first term.
Iran has repeatedly dismissed the sanctions policy as a failure, insisting that economic pressure and threats will not force it to change course.

Unknown

16:44:30 UTC
01:44:30 KST

Heavy rain brought by a low-pressure system and strong southwesterly winds triggered widespread flooding, landslides and damage across central, southern and eastern Taiwan yesterday, disrupting travel and prompting mass evacuations.
As of 6pm yesterday, torrential rains had left one person dead in Tainan, four missing — one each in Tainan and Pingtung County and two in Hualien County — and 155 injured nationwide, the Central Emergency Operation Center said.
The center added that 4,263 people were evacuated across the nation: 2,649 in Kaohsiung, 765 in Pingtung County, 567 in Tainan, 224 in Hualien County, 46 in Taitung County and 12 in Chiayi County.
Photo courtesy of a member of the public
In Kaohsiung, continuous downpours caused roads to collapse in Cianjhen (前鎮), Renwu (仁武) and Gangshan (岡山) districts, including a sinkhole 3m long, 2m wide and 1.2m deep on Cianjhen’s Guangsi Road.
In Tianliao District (田寮), a landslide on a road near Neian Bridge on Sunday afternoon left more than 30 residents temporarily stranded before clearance operations began.
Pingtung County reported severe urban and agricultural flooding, particularly in Wandan (萬丹), Chaojhou (潮州) and Donggang (東港) townships, where water levels reached thigh-high on several major roads.
Photo courtesy of the Lioujia District Office
In Tainan, 24-hour accumulated rainfall exceeded 400mm in Yongkang (永康) and Rende (仁德) districts.
Rising water levels along the Sanye River (三爺溪) caused flooding in low-lying areas, forcing the temporary closure of both ramps to Rende Interchange on Freeway No. 1.
As the roads near An Nan Hospital were also inundated, firefighters used inflatable boats to transport about 200 people seeking medical treatment.
Continuous rain also caused a side wall of the Great East Gate, a national historic site constructed in 1725, to collapse early yesterday morning after rainwater seeped into its base.
In Hualien County, several southern townships recorded more than 300mm of rainfall, and surging water in the Siouguluan River (秀姑巒溪) washed away the temporary Yuchang access road connecting Yuli (玉里) and Changliang (長良).
Firefighters were searching for a hospital security guard who was reported missing after his mobile phone signal was last detected near the crossing.
Authorities also closed several mountain roads and temporary bridge crossings in southern Hualien as a precaution.
Nearby, at the Wanli River (萬里溪) barrier lake, the water level dropped by 4.7m, reducing its volume by about 1 million tonnes. Nonetheless, authorities maintained a red alert for the river channel. All 209 people in the evacuation zone around the river landslide-dammed lake have been evacuated.
Heavy rain is forecast to continue across most of the country through this morning, with torrential rainfall likely in the southern and southeastern areas due to strong southwesterly winds and multiple weather systems, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said.

A third storm, Narra, near Vietnam yesterday, is not expected to directly affect Taiwan, the CWA said.

Teng entered in the fifth inning with one out and a runner on first after the Athletics erased a six-run deficit to tie the game 6-6.
The 27-year-old faced seven batters, allowing one hit and hitting one batter while throwing 28 pitches. Four of his five outs came on strikeouts, and his fastball topped out at 94.3 miles per hour.
Photo: AP
Teng’s sweeper was particularly effective. He threw the pitch 16 times, inducing seven misses on 10 swings, a 70 percent miss rate.
After throwing a hit-by-pitch and a wild pitch to put Athletics runners on second and third base, Teng ended the fifth with a strikeout. He returned for a scoreless sixth, working around a double while adding two more strikeouts.
Steven Okert replaced Teng and surrendered a go-ahead solo home run to Max Muncy in the seventh, which proved decisive in Houston’s 7-6 loss.
Teng was recalled from Triple-A on Friday, having last appeared in the majors about a month earlier before being optioned on July 26.
During his latest stint in Triple-A, Teng worked exclusively as a reliever, posting a 3.48 ERA with 15 strikeouts and three walks over 10-1/3 innings. He is expected to continue pitching out of Houston’s bullpen.
Teng, who had a 5-6 record in the majors, improved his ERA to 4.24 after the game.

16:44:30 UTC

The inaugural Taiwan Exercise Recovery Technique Open is being held in Taoyuan this weekend, bringing together almost 100 practitioners from Taiwan and elsewhere in Asia, organizers said yesterday.
The competition, also referred to as the Taiwan Sports Recovery Championship, is taking place alongside the International Sports Massage Master Forum at National Taiwan Sport University.
The competition has attracted participants from Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong and Malaysia and is the first of its kind to be held in Taiwan, according to its organizers, the Taiwan Exercise Recovery Association.
Photo: CNA
The 95 entrants are competing in four categories: sport-specific massage, freestyle manual techniques, tool-assisted methods and sports aromatherapy.
At a news conference in Taipei on Monday, Canadian sports massage specialist Matthew Chalons, who has more than 13 years of practical and teaching experience, said physical fatigue accumulates during training, making recovery essential to helping the body adapt and prepare for its next challenge.
The association said it hoped the event would provide a platform for practitioners to exchange knowledge, build up Taiwan’s sports recovery industry and expand their international connections.
The association certified Taiwan’s first group of qualified sports massage competition judges during the news conference.
The judges completed training and assessments developed to improve professional standards and credibility in Taiwan’s sports massage and bodywork sectors, the association said.

NT dollar advance loses support as equity inflows fade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:27 UTC
01:44:27 KST

The New Taiwan dollar’s strongest monthly rise in over a year is running into a storm of headwinds, sowing doubts among analysts on the sustainability of its rebound.
A drop in foreign equity inflows, a forward market implying underlying demand has softened and some technical resistance levels have led some analysts to rethink the prospect of future gains. That is impairing this month’s advance which had set the currency on course for its best month since May last year, following its worst month in 11 years last month.
“Foreign equity inflow impulse has faded after the mid-Aug buying,” Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp (華僑銀行) foreign exchange strategist Christopher Wong (黃經隆) said in Singapore. He said the forwards market has not widened materially, suggesting local exporters are not betting on a NT dollar rally.
Photo: AFP
Wong added that while 31.80 serves as near-term support for the currency pair, a more decisive drop would require a broader weakness in the US dollar, alongside renewed foreign capital inflows and stronger US dollar-conversion activity by exporters.
Much of the NT dollar’s rally this month came as outflows from dividend repatriation dwindled, bringing investor focus back to Taiwan’s robust economic fundamentals driven by the tech sector. The NT dollar closed 0.02 percent lower at 31.854 per US dollar yesterday.
However, even as net inflows recovered from a slump last month, analysts are warning that the local currency lacks the fresh capital flow for it to return to pre selloff levels. Inflows slowed to about US$861 million last week from US$6.5 billion in the prior week.
“Dollar-Taiwan dollar has been tracking equity flows nicely throughout this year, until the recent moves,” Australia & New Zealand Banking Group head of Asia research Khoon Goh (吳昆) said.
“Part of the move could be pullback after the July dividend repatriation flows were done,” he said, adding that “unless there is ongoing large equity inflows, it looks like further downside in dollar-Taiwan dollar should be limited.”
The move in the actively traded one week non-deliverable forward points underscores cooling optimism for the NT dollar. After spending earlier this month in negative territory, the points have drifted back toward neutral levels since mid-month, signaling reduced confidence in the currency’s ability to sustain future gains.
“31.77 is a key support level though, and we may see more two-way action, especially if the dollar starts to make a more meaningful rebound,” Malayan Banking Berhad senior foreign exchange strategist Fiona Lim (林梅玲) said.
Lim said that she does not rule out forward points shifting back into positive terrain — a move that would price in New Taiwan dollar weakness — should hedging demand rise or the US dollar rebound.

China ‘all bark, no bite’ in maritime incidents: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:27 UTC
01:44:27 KST

Two Chinese maritime actions near Taiwan this month demonstrate Beijing’s efforts to expand its reach and challenge the international order, a national security source said yesterday.
In the first action, China’s Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration said it would impose “traffic controls” on vessels in the Taiwan Strait during Typhoon Dolphin. In the second, Beijing held joint naval exercises with the Indonesian Navy east of Taiwan.
In both incidents, China was “all bark and no bite,” using low-intensity actions and cognitive warfare as part of its broader efforts to expand its reach and challenge the international order, the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Photo: Screen grab from warship_cam’s X account sourced from X-@weiqi_xiulang
On Aug. 5, Beijing announced “traffic controls” north and south of the Taiwan Strait, citing typhoon-related safety precautions, ordering vessels passing through the area to follow instructions from Chinese maritime authorities.
However, the Taiwan Strait is international waters, and Beijing’s move openly challenged established international norms, including those under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the source said.
The Maritime and Port Bureau and Mainland Affairs Council condemned the move as an attempt by China to expand its authority, while the US Department of State said it opposed actions that interfered with freedom of navigation in the Taiwan Strait.
In practice, the Chinese measures amounted to little more than maritime broadcasts and ended with the typhoon, the source said.
A week later, on Aug. 12, China unilaterally announced that it had conducted a “joint exercise” with an Indonesian Navy destroyer in waters east of Taiwan.
The Indonesian warship, the KRI I Gusti Ngurah Rai (332), was returning from Vladivostok, Russia, where it had participated in exercises with the Russian Navy, and later conducted drills with Japan near Tokyo, according to media reports.
Indonesia said its vessel had merely conducted a “passing exercise” with the Chinese navy while returning home from Russia.
The source said the China-Indonesia activities were essentially communication drills in which vessels exchange greetings and test communications procedures while passing in international waters.
However, China deliberately portrayed the interactions as formal naval exercises, in an attempt to give the impression that Beijing has substantive jurisdiction over waters east of Taiwan and that Indonesia sides with China on issues related to Taiwan, the source said.
Beijing also sought to use Indonesia to reinforce its position regarding overlapping maritime claims and disputed waters around Japan and the Philippines, they said.
In both incidents, China sought to communicate the message that it is enforcing the law and maintaining a presence around Taiwan, they said.
Beijing used low-intensity actions to wage high-profile cognitive warfare, testing boundaries and challenging international order while attempting to avoid provoking excessive backlash, they said.
Following the incidents, the US made clear that it did not want China to undermine peace and stability in the region, while urging other countries not to amplify Beijing’s destabilizing narratives or endorse its unilateral actions, but instead to operate within the framework of international norms, the source said.
The waterways around Taiwan constitute two of the world’s most important arteries for high-tech supply chains, making Beijing’s “gray zone” activities an “immediate and clear threat” to countries around the world, which is a key reason the US responded repeatedly within a short period, they said.

Unemployment sees usual school-related increase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:26 UTC
01:44:26 KST

Taiwan’s unemployment rate rose to 3.39 percent last month from 3.34 percent in June, as new graduates and students entered the labor market, although the increase was largely seasonal, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said yesterday.
Last month’s figure remained the lowest July reading since 2001, highlighting the resilience of a labor market supported by strong economic growth, DGBAS said.
“The rise in unemployment was largely seasonal,” Department of Census deputy director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) said. “The graduation season brought more new graduates into the job market, while some students also sought temporary work during the summer vacation.”
Photo courtesy of the Taipei Department of Labor
The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate held steady at 3.33 percent, indicating little change in underlying employment conditions, the agency said.
The number of unemployed people increased by 7,000 from June to 409,000, while employment rose as students, and new graduates entered the workforce during the summer vacation.
Consequently, the labor force expanded to 12.06 million, pushing the participation rate up 0.1 percentage points to 59.66 percent, the highest for July in 35 years, Tan said.
By educational attainment, the unemployment rate was highest among people with university degrees at 4.54 percent, followed by those with senior-high-school or vocational-high-school education at 3.11 percent and those with graduate degrees at 2.97 percent.
Among age groups, the unemployment rate for people aged 15 to 24 was 11.71 percent, as many were first-time job seekers entering the labor market during the graduation season and adjusting to the workplace. The rate was 5.82 percent among those aged 25 to 29 and 3.29 percent among those aged 30 to 34.
The seasonal increase in unemployment is expected to continue this month as the summer vacation continues, with the jobless rate possibly rising above last month’s levels, Tan said.
The rate should begin to ease next month as graduates find jobs and students return to school, she said.
The seasonal movement is tied to academic tides rather than deterioration in labor-market conditions, she said.
Underemployment remained confined to a relatively narrow range. The number of people working fewer hours than they wanted rose by 1,000 from June to 122,000, Tan said.
The figure has ranged between 115,000 and 122,000 since the start of the year, with no sign of sharp deterioration, she said.
For the first seven months, the average unemployment rate was 3.32 percent, down 0.02 percentage point from a year earlier.

EDITORIAL: AI boom shines light on inequality gap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:23 UTC
01:44:23 KST

Last year, the nation’s average household disposable income rose 3.9 percent year-on-year to a record NT$1.21 million (US$37,986), but the income ratio of the highest-earning 20 percent and the lowest-earning 20 percent widened to 6.17, the highest in 14 years, from 6.14 in the previous year, data released earlier this month by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) showed.
The average disposable income among the top 20 percent of households increased 3.9 percent to NT$2.45 million last year from the previous year, and that of the bottom 20 percent rose 3.5 percent to NT$397,000. That divide likely reflects a booming stock market, strong tech industry performance driven by demand for semiconductors and artificial intelligence (AI) products, and widening wage disparities across industries, even as Taiwan’s GDP grew 8.76 percent last year.
Structural differences across counties and cities also contribute to income disparities. For example, many technology professionals who live in Hsinchu city and county and work in the Hsinchu Science Park bring home more income from bonuses and overtime pay due to the high concentration of major tech firms in the region, while some households in Taipei receive income from dividends and rent. Unsurprisingly, out of Taiwan’s 22 administrative regions, Hsinchu City was the richest last year, followed by Hsinchu County, with average annual household incomes of NT$2.04 million and NT$2.01 million, respectively, while Taipei ranked third at NT$1.9 million. In comparison, the national average rose 3.3 percent to a record NT$1.53 million last year from a year earlier, the data showed.
The average income in Miaoli County was NT$1.4 million last year, ranking it ninth-richest in Taiwan, ahead of Tainan’s NT$1.3 million. Previously, the county never broke the top 10 for household income, but following investments by tech firms such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, Micron Technology Inc and MediaTek Inc — as well as that many tech employees live in the county’s Jhunan (竹南) or Toufen (頭份) townships because of the lower housing costs and commute to the Hsinchu Science Park — Miaoli’s income ranking has significantly improved over the past few years.
Rising household incomes in Hsinchu city and county and Miaoli County reflect the emergence of high-income clusters in Taiwan, as the nation’s semiconductor industry has gained a strong foothold globally and local tech firms are benefiting from growing AI-related business opportunities. However, imbalanced regional development and uneven industrial progress persist, and the income gap between Hsinchu city and county and other areas continues to widen.
Economic growth can come with income inequality, and during economic downturns, that gap can widen further, with low-income households bearing the brunt of it. For example, during the 2008-2009 global financial crisis, the disposable income of the highest-earning 20 percent of households shrank 2.43 percent from the previous year, but the lowest-earning 20 percent faced a larger 7 percent decrease, with the income ratio rising to 6.34 from 6.05 a year earlier, DGBAS data showed.
The government has in the past sought to address income inequality through social welfare and healthcare reforms. However, amid global supply chain restructuring and a profound industrial transformation driven by AI, how to effectively resolve the imbalance between economic growth and income distribution will be a crucial challenge for Taiwan.
The government has used vouchers, cash handouts, rental subsidies and family support schemes over the past decade to aid low-income households. However, beyond temporary cash support, government policies should also focus on enhancing the income-generating capacity of young people, the service sector and minority households in seeking long-term gains.
Tamkang University banking and finance professor Lee Wo-chiang (李沃牆) said that the government’s plan for another universal cash handout to share the economic benefits of AI with the public might please Taiwanese, but it does not address widening income inequality. He said the government should help small and medium-sized enterprises, traditional industries and the service sector to use AI to reduce the costs of digital transformation. In addition, the government should do more to promote digital education and AI-focused vocational training for low-skilled workers, while transforming the gains brought by AI into social investment to reduce the cost of living for low and middle-income families, thereby narrowing the income gap.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

No comfort zone, no complacency: PSG coach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:23 UTC
01:44:23 KST

Paris Saint-Germain players cannot afford to cruise through the season, as coach Luis Enrique said he expected them to play out of their comfort zone.
The PSG coach took Ousmane Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia off at halftime of their opening game of the new Ligue 1 season, bringing on Mika Godts and Ferran Torres, who scored twice to salvage a point at Stade Rennais on Sunday.
“Football is like that. Paris Saint-Germain have won nothing, nothing,” he said of the new season where they defend not only their Ligue 1 title but chase a third successive Champions League victory. “If you think about what you’ve won, you’re not going to win anything! There is no credit. You have to show every day, every match, every training session, that you’re ready. Otherwise, it’s easy to relax and start slipping.”
Photo: REuters
“I wasn’t brought up that way,” he said. “We are always looking to win, and to keep winning, you have to step outside your comfort zone. Is that clear?”

Ministry to expand budget for mental health program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:22 UTC
01:44:22 KST

The government’s mental health support program for young people and middle-aged adults has resulted in about 28 percent of the beneficiaries receiving further mental health services, the Ministry of Health and Welfare (MOHW) said yesterday, adding that it would propose an expanded budget for the program next year.
Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said at an event held by the Taiwan Primary Care Association on Sunday that the central government general budget proposed for next year is about NT$3.9 trillion (US$122.4 billion).
Among the general budget proposal, about NT$60 billion would be allocated to the National Health Insurance system, NT$10 billion to the Healthy Taiwan Cultivation Plan and about NT$429 million for the mental health support program, he said.
Photo: Lin Hui-chin, Taipei Times
The mental health support program was launched on Aug. 1, 2024, offering people aged 15 to 45 up to three free psychological counseling sessions.
Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) yesterday said the program’s user satisfaction is high, and the number of beneficiaries continues to grow.
Statistics show that since the program was launched, about 28 percent of the beneficiaries were referred to mental health services, receiving follow-up care and treatment, Shih said.
The budget for the program was approximately NT$350 million this year, but, as the demand is still growing, the ministry proposed to expand the budget to NT$429 million next year, which would cover about 100,000 beneficiaries, he said.
The ministry has other mental health support measures covering other age groups as well, such as free counseling sessions for people with cancer and their family, and the implementation of the WHO’s Integrated Care for Older People evaluation for people aged 65 or above under the Long-Term Care 3.0 program.
The health ministry would also collaborate with the Ministry of the Interior to launch a new care program, making home visits to care for older people living alone, a subset of about 700,000 to 750,000 people, and introducing care services based on their risk levels.
Meanwhile, asked about the effectiveness of opening urgent care centers across the nation, Shih said that some centers have exceptionally higher service volumes, such as a center in Tainan, so the city is planning to set up another urgent care center.
However, the service volume at a center in Taipei is relatively low, so the Taipei Department of Health is evaluating whether it should move the center to a different location or enhance its publicity, he said.
The ministry on Nov. 2 last year launched a urgent care center pilot program to provide urgent medical care to people with mild to moderate symptoms at 13 centers in the nation’s six special municipalities on weekends and holidays to help reduce pressure on crowded emergency rooms.

Taipei leads the rise in average life expectancy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:21 UTC
01:44:21 KST

Taiwan’s average life expectancy climbed to 81.27 last year from 80.77 a year earlier, with Taipei recording the longest average at 83.98, the Ministry of the Interior said yesterday.
Despite the year-on-year rise, Taiwan’s national average life expectancy had not yet returned to the pre-COVID-19 peak of 81.32 in 2020, the ministry said.
However, it is higher than the global average of 73.5, it added.
The number of deaths last year moved lower for the third consecutive year, as the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic eased, down 1,674 from a year earlier to 199,639, the ministry said.
The number of deaths aged 65 or older was 151,936 last year, accounting for 76.1 percent of the national total.
The average crude death rate slid 0.005 percentage points from a year earlier to 0.885 percent, it said.
The average life expectancy of women and men in Taiwan rose 0.45 years and 0.51 years from a year earlier to 84.75 and 77.93 respectively, the ministry said.
Average life expectancy for women in Taiwan returned to the pre-COVID-19 peak of 84.74 in 2020, but the average among men did not return to 2020’s peak of 78.11, it said.
The average for both women and men in Taiwan was higher than the global average of 76.2 years and 70.9 years respectively.
Taipei led in average life expectancy, rising from 83.4 in 2024 to 83.98 last year, ahead of Hsinchu City (82.13 years) and New Taipei City (81.54 years).
Taitung County had the lowest average life expectancy at 76.49 years. It was the only administrative area in Taiwan to report a figure below 77.
Taipei also recorded the highest life expectancy of 86.74 years among women, ahead of Hsinchu City’s 85.2 years.
The capital also had the highest average life expectancy of 81.1 years among men, followed by Hsinchu City at 79.1 years.
Taitung reported the lowest average life expectancy of 81.54 years for women and 72.3 years for men, the data showed.
The latest statistics about individual administrative areas excluded Kinmen County, which saw a large population outflow, and Lienchiang County, the ministry said.

Taiwan finding diplomatic space in Europe: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:21 UTC
01:44:21 KST

Sister-city arrangements, memoranda of understanding and regular exchange mechanisms could become important channels for Taiwan, even as its formal diplomatic space in the region remains constrained, the Central European Institute of Asian Studies said in a report.
Taiwan has in the past few years expanded its international activity through exchanges with local governments, as most European countries maintain a “one China” policy, the report said, adding that such local-level exchanges can serve as an important complement to formal diplomacy.
Such cooperation can also raise Taiwan’s visibility and increase participation in the international community, it added.
Photo: Reuters
Local Taiwanese governments have 33 cooperative relationships with European cities, towns or regional governments, according to the report.
Poland has the most, with seven cities — including Warsaw, Katowice, Gdynia and Poznan — having established ties with Taiwan, while Germany has five such arrangements, including with Dresden, the think tank said.
Taiwan’s strengths in semiconductors, information and communications technology, smart manufacturing and technological innovation have made it an important partner for local European governments seeking to diversify supply chains and reduce their dependence on China, it said.
Dresden has held exchanges with Kaohsiung and Hsinchu City in talent development and industrial cooperation, partly driven by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co’s plans to establish a semiconductor plant in the German city.
However, Taiwan’s subnational diplomatic ties in Europe remain relatively limited compared with the more than 100 local partnerships it has in the US and more than 34 in Japan, the report said.
One reason is the relatively small size of Taiwan’s overseas communities in Europe, it said.
Germany has the largest Taiwanese population in Europe with about 8,000 people, but that is far fewer than in the US or Japan, the institute said.
The absence of a large overseas community and strong civil society networks means there is less grassroots momentum to promote and advance local-level initiatives, it said.
Some European cities are concerned about the possibility of political or economic retaliation from China for working with Taiwan, it said.
For example, Edinburgh, Scotland, had planned to sign a friendship-city agreement with Kaohsiung in 2024, but withdrew the proposal after a Chinese diplomat warned of possible “serious consequences,” the report said, adding that local universities, businesses and the tourism sector also expressed concerns about the potential impact on their access to the Chinese market.
By contrast, Prague has demonstrated greater resilience to such pressure, it said.
The Czech capital ended its sister-city agreement with Beijing in 2019 over a dispute involving a “one China” clause and established a partnership with Taipei in 2020, it said.
Despite subsequent Chinese measures restricting cultural exchanges, Prague continued to deepen cooperation with Taiwan, making it an important example of subnational engagement with Taiwan in Europe, the institute said.
At least 71 cities or regions simultaneously maintain relationships with Taiwanese and Chinese cities, it said.
For example, Warsaw has ties with Taipei and Harbin, China, while Bratislava Region, a self-governing administrative region of Slovakia, maintains relations with Kaohsiung and Shanghai, the report said.
Such arrangements have rarely resulted in substantive Chinese retaliation, it said.
Taiwan should focus on deepening partnerships by regularly reviewing the relationships, strengthening the participation of universities, chambers of commerce and businesses, and establishing mechanisms to track progress, it said.
That would help transform sister-city relationships from largely symbolic exchanges into concrete forms of cooperation, it said.
Taiwan should also use existing multilateral platforms, including the annual Smart City Summit and Expo and the Pact of Free Cities to engage with more European local governments and expand its international network, the report said.
Enhancing coordination between central and local governments, leveraging Taiwan’s industrial and technological strengths, and turning partnerships into substantive cooperation could further expand Taiwan’s international participation in Europe, it added.

Taipower planning for AI power demand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:20 UTC
01:44:20 KST

Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) plans to supply electricity to artificial intelligence (AI) data centers through direct lines, as rising AI demand puts pressure on the grid, Taipower chairman Tseng Wen-sheng (曾文生) said on Sunday.
The utility plans to allow AI data center operators to manage those dedicated power lines themselves, with their length, costs and timing determined by market mechanisms, Tseng said during an interview.
“The most stable way to supply electricity is to locate as close to the power source as possible,” Tseng said.
Photo: Peter Lo, Taipei Times
Electricity is a “sovereign industry,” and Taiwan needs to reinforce the resilience of its power supply amid geopolitical risks, he said.
Taipower has discussed future power demand with the Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association to get a clear picture of the industry’s electricity consumption, Tseng said, to ensure there would be sufficient power to meet the industry’s demand.
Following a major power outage on March 3, 2022, Taipower reviewed its grid and introduced measures to increase resilience, including plans to connect power plants with science parks, Tseng said.
Rather than routing electricity through the main north-south transmission grid, Taipower is developing dedicated lines to ease congestion and diversify risks, he said.
Examples include links from the Datan Power Plant (大潭電廠) in Taoyuan’s Guanyin District (觀音) to the Taoyuan Aerotropolis, and from the Tunghsiao Power Plant (通霄電廠) in Miaoli County to the Hsinchu Science Park (新竹科學園區), he said.
Grid resilience has become a key part of supplying the semiconductor industry amid the AI boom, he said.
Tseng said Taipower has shifted from focusing primarily on overall electricity supply to matching major power users with available generation and grid capacity, tracking demand at individual factories and science parks to plan supply more precisely.
AI data centers across the world face challenges such as location controls, pricing mechanisms, capacity thresholds and requirements for self-generated power, he said.
Growing power demand requires upgrades to the grid, including higher voltage levels, greater cable capacity and underground infrastructure overhaul, he added.

Xiaomi develops its own AI mobile chip in challenge to Qualcomm, MediaTek
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:19 UTC
01:44:19 KST

Xiaomi Corp (小米) launched a mobile processor for its marquee devices, putting pressure on Qualcomm Inc and MediaTek Inc (聯發科) which for years supplied the key component to the Chinese company.
The Xring O3 system-on-a-chip advances Xiaomi’s in-house semiconductor design efforts with more power-efficient image processing and better artificial intelligence capabilities, the Beijing-based company said in a post on Chinese social media platform Weibo yesterday.
Xiaomi’s new silicon is made using a 3-nanometer fabrication process, according to a WeChat post by founder Lei Jun (雷軍). That’s closer to the node used for Apple Inc’s most recent A19 Pro chips and well ahead of its biggest home rival Huawei Technologies Co’s (華為) in-house designs. Xiaomi has contracted Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) to manufacture the chips, Reuters reported.
Photo: Bloomberg
San Diego, California-based Qualcomm and Taiwan’s MediaTek have long provided Xiaomi’s key processors. The Chinese company, which also designs and produces electric vehicles, is building on years of its own research on semiconductors to lower reliance on foreign chips. Having an in-house chip for its flagship products would strengthen Xiaomi’s bargaining position with suppliers and boost its consumer appeal in a fiercely competitive market.
Rival Huawei uses self-developed Kirin processors in its premium phones after a series of US restrictions cut it off from key global suppliers including Qualcomm. In contrast, Xiaomi isn’t subject to sanctions preventing it from contracting with international suppliers.
Once China’s No. 1 smartphone maker, Xiaomi is grappling with lackluster demand for both its handset and electric-vehicle businesses as countrywide consumption levels stagnate.
In smartphones, the company suffered the heaviest shipment decline among major hardware makers in the June quarter, according to Counterpoint Research. Investors are also concerned that aggressive pricing for its latest sport utility vehicles could further squeeze margins.
The Xring O3 chip is expected to power Xiaomi’s upcoming flagship folding phone, with a shipment target of 200,000 to 300,000 units, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Automatic subscription renewals to be banned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:19 UTC
01:44:19 KST

The government would soon require digital service providers to stop automatically renewing subscriptions, and allow users to manually select and confirm renewals by checking a clearly labeled box, the Executive Yuan said yesterday.
The issue was first raised by Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Legislator Liao Hsien-hsiang (廖先翔).
The use of digital subscription systems has expanded from streaming media to other services, but service providers often design user interfaces in such ways that make it easy to subscribe but difficult to cancel subscriptions, Liao said.
Photo: Hsu Tzu-ling, Taipei Times
Service providers hide automatic subscription renewal clauses in the contract, having the consent box pre-ticked and complicating the subscription cancelation procedures, he said.
People could unknowingly sustain financial losses this way, and have no recourse for the problem as many of the digital service providers are based overseas, he said, adding that the Executive Yuan should propose solutions within one month.
The Cabinet said that the Ministry of Digital Affairs could amend the Mandatory and Prohibited Clauses for Standard Contracts in Online Retail Transactions (零售業等網路交易定型化契約應記載及不得記載事項) to address the problem.
The amendment would require businesses to clearly disclose important information, including the renewal period, fees and cancelation procedures, before consumers agree to a subscription, it said.
Businesses would be prohibited from using pre-ticked boxes or other mechanisms presuming users’ consent to automatic payments, and must provide a clearly labeled box for them to manually check and confirm their consent, the Cabinet said.
Cancelation procedures must be as convenient as the subscription process, it added.
A new provision in the contract would prohibit businesses from including terms that presume consumers’ consent to automatic subscription renewals and charges, and oblige them to separately notify users before an automatic renewal payment is charged, it said.
If a business conceals such information, it may be fined NT$50,000 to NT$25 million (US$1,570 to US$784,831) under Article 42 of the Fair Trade Act (公平交易法). If the business fails to correct the issue by the given deadline, it may be fined NT$100,000 to NT$50 million per contravention, the Executive Yuan said.
Businesses must provide consumers with sufficient and accurate information about how to subscribe to, pay for and cancel digital subscription services, as required under the Consumer Protection Act (消費者保護法), it said.
If the terms are presented in a way that makes them difficult for users to notice or understand, the terms do not constitute part of the contract under Article 12 of the Enforcement Rules of Consumer Protection Act (消費者保護法施行細則), and consumers may claim that they are not bound by them, it added.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
16:44:13 UTC
01:44:13 KST

Nine people, including employees of Nvidia and Super Micro, have been indicted over illegal exports of artificial intelligence (AI) servers to China, the Keelung District Prosecutors’ Office said yesterday.
Semiconductor powerhouse Taiwan is the world’s largest producer of advanced chips used in AI applications. Prosecutors this year investigated the suspected illegal export of servers equipped with Nvidia chips subject to US export controls.
Washington has imposed curbs since 2022, making it illegal for such semiconductors to be exported or sold in China without a license.
Photo: Reuters
Eight people, including one employee of Nvidia’s Taiwan unit and two employees of Super Micro’s Taiwan unit, were charged with breach of trust and document forgery in connection with the illegal export of high-end AI servers, Keelung prosecutors said in a statement.
Neither company immediately responded to requests for comment.
A ninth defendant was charged in a related case involving the alleged siphoning of funds from a distributor company involved, the statement said, without providing the full names of any of the defendants.
The alleged scheme involved making it appear that 130 B300 servers ordered from Super Micro would be installed and used at a rented server facility in Taiwan.
Prosecutors said false end-user documents stated that the servers would be installed in Taiwan.
Of those 130 servers, 74 were ultimately exported and delivered to Chinese customers through routes that included direct shipments to China, as well as transshipments through Indonesia, Japan and Hong Kong, they said.
The remaining 56 servers were intended to be exported to a company in Japan, prosecutors said, but Taiwanese customs officials detected irregularities and stopped their export.
The prosecutors said the defendants were “fully aware” that Nvidia and Super Micro have “rigorous internal control procedures” regarding exports.
However, the defendants “colluded with one another at various levels for enormous profit, illegally exporting high-end servers, increasing corporate compliance costs, and severely damaging our nation’s international image,” they added.
Taiwan has tightened export controls in the past few years to keep advanced technology and know-how from reaching China.

A cross-party group of Japanese lawmakers, including one from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s governing party, yesterday headed to Beijing to meet with Chinese officials for the first time since ties between the two Asian rivals deteriorated after Takaichi’s comment on Taiwan angered China.
The group, which includes Gaku Hashimoto, a lawmaker of Takaichi’s governing Liberal Democratic Party and a former health and welfare vice minister, and a lawmaker each from two opposition parties Komeito and the Centrist Reform Alliance (CRA), is to meet with Chinese Communist Party officials during their visit through Thursday.

Photo: AFP
Isa, who has served as a diplomat at the Japanese embassy in China, wrote on X earlier this month that bilateral ties have sunk to their worst since the 1972 normalization of relations.
He wrote that officials had always remained in communication even during previous lows: “Now all channels between officials and ministries have been cut off.”
The situation is not in the national interest of either side, Isa said at the time, and the Chinese side accepted a request from Japanese lawmakers for a “window for dialogue.”
Soon after taking office, Takaichi said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute “a survival-threatening situation” for Japan that would justify the use of force, enraging Beijing.
The remark crossed what China considers a red line in its relations with other countries about Taiwan.
Takaichi has not retracted her comment, but when marking Japan’s World War II surrender on Aug. 15, she prayed remotely instead of visiting the controversial Yasukuni Shrine, seen by China and South Korea as lacking remorse for Japan’s wartime militarism and atrocities.

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴) raised HK$80 billion (US$10.2 billion) in Hong Kong’s biggest follow-on offering, underscoring its willingness to amass and spend vast sums to take the lead in global artificial intelligence (AI).
The online retail giant-turned-AI player sold 710 million shares at HK$112.70 each and its stock slumped 8.5 percent yesterday, the most since early 2025. Still, the deal — which was priced at a 3.6 percent discount to the Friday close of Alibaba’s US-traded shares — attracted demand from institutional investors for almost three times the offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Alibaba will be subject to a lockup of 90 days.
The capital raising reflects Alibaba’s eagerness to outspend and outrun Chinese rivals in the chase to define the frontier of AI development. Among country’s big technology firms, Alibaba has come closest to the huge outlays of its US peers. The company has sold off assets and pledged to spend more than 380 billion yuan (US$56.5 billion) over three years on AI, from chips and data centers to large-language model development. Its flagship Qwen (通義千問) offering is now the world’s most popular model family.
Photo: Reuters
Alibaba’s top two executives both purchased company shares yesterday. Chairman Joseph Tsai (蔡崇信) purchased about HK$80 million worth of shares, while chief executive officer Eddie Wu (吳泳銘) acquired about HK$40 million, according to filings with the Hong Kong stock exchange.
The share issue is a departure from Alibaba’s years-long efforts to improve shareholder returns, Union Bancaire Privee SA managing director Vey-Sern Ling (凌煒森) said.
“Why not bonds?” he asked. “It tells me that they may need more funds than we expect for AI investments and also they may be rushing to be ahead of other companies.”
Chinese AI leaders have so far shown restraint relative to American tech providers like Meta Platforms Inc and Alphabet Inc, who’ve together earmarked trillions of dollars in a bid to stay ahead. Alibaba’s home rival Baidu Inc (百度) has no plan for a new share issuance, as its existing funds and operating cash flow are sufficient, a company spokesperson said yesterday.
But the competition is intensifying, prices for hardware such as memory chips are skyrocketing, and companies fear missing out on revolutionary technology.
Alibaba’s concentrated effort to challenge Anthropic PBC and OpenAI is already eroding margins, while anemic domestic consumption dogs its mainstay online retail business. The company amped up its capital spending in the June quarter to nearly US$10 billion and said it’s putting the focus on long-term competitiveness.
Some investors question whether Alibaba is getting enough for its capital. Its cloud-computing division is racking up double-digit percentage growth and AI-related revenue gains are in triple-digit territory. But like many of its peers, Alibaba has yet to show how it will derive sustainable, longer-term revenue from AI services.
The size of Alibaba’s equity raise is “significant,” but possible demand from financial institutions and sovereign-wealth funds should soften some concerns about dilution, Saxo Markets chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said.
“The bigger question is how Alibaba monetizes this spend” given weak Chinese consumer sentiment and intense competition in the country’s AI market, she said. Alibaba intends to use the proceeds to invest in full-stack AI capabilities, including by expanding and enhancing its infrastructure.
